utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Happy New Year, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceeding in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it because his microphone is not on? Could I ask you to repeat, Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And Happy New Year as well from the Prosecution. It's Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, Case Manager. In today the rarefied heights, Courtroom I, I note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. And appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin. And Madam Registrar, please, could you move all the stuff. I can't see Mr. Ackerman, I can't see anyone from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Happy New Year, Your Honour. I'm David Cunningham with John Ackerman and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. And I wish you a Happy New Year on my own behalf. And on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya, I wish happy new year to each and every one of you. Thank you. I suppose there are a few preliminaries. What is the situation with regard to the witnesses that we are expected to hear this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Witness 21 is here and ready. Witness 69 will be here and testify on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have a problem on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Because I had -- going back I don't know how many weeks, but before the -- let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour, I can't for one moment tell you anything about him, until we get a summary knowing exactly what he's going to talk about and what he's going to say, I can't tell you anything about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I understand there are going to be videolinks on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to Dmitrasinovic, the summary provided by Mr. Golic and the testimony of Mr. Golic is a pretty effective disclosure of what he's going to take about. It will be almost identical testimony. We are going to file a motion today to have Witness Number 49 testify by videolink. When we last saw him, his health was not good, but he believed he could travel here if he could be driven here by car and back. His health apparently has now deteriorated to the point where that's not practical for him either. We have medical certificates for both Witness 49 and 48. They haven't been translated. I have them here in the original language. One's in German; one's in Serbian. I can give you copies in those languages, or you can wait until I get them back from CLSS. We were able to receive them only yesterday. And that should, Your Honour, if we can put things together on Wednesday, we should finish the Brdjanin witnesses with the exception of the expert who is scheduled for 9 February, this week. We should be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about Thursday? What's going to happen on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it may be that if Dmitrasinovic is only a one-day witness, and I think he should be, we could skip Wednesday, put him on Thursday, and then you wouldn't have to worry about Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem as I explained, for this special event, we will have to travel to Amsterdam. And we are all going to travel together, but I don't know exactly what time we're coming back. We could still start Wednesday afternoon, and I think that will be a safer bet for everyone. I mean, I would prefer having it that way. I mean starting Wednesday afternoon, and that way we'll make sure that the witness -- we'll finish with the witness by the end of Thursday, if that is okay with you. I mean, otherwise we would be taking a risk supposedly if we start with the witness on Thursday, not knowing whether we would be in a position to finish him on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only risk we would have to take is he might have to stay until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a problem for me or any of us three. Yeah, we could do that. I mean, the easiest way of going about it is to miss Wednesday altogether. That's the easiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine with me. I think we can finish him on Thursday. My recollection is we finished Mr. Golic in one day, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember, Mr. Ackerman. I honestly don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm quite certain we did. We should have no trouble finishing him on Thursday, I think. So if we just skip Wednesday, I think we're still on track to complete everything this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask now, whoever is responsible, because I don't know what the situation will be like and what the problems that could arise would be. If -- we had made arrangements for the testimony of Mr. Dmitrasinovic -- no, sorry, Witness 48 to testify by videolink on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's going through now I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 48 and 49 both, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with 48. Because the preparations we had made were for 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you expect that to last.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those are both one-hour directs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One-hour direct. And you haven't seen any statements --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's all very well for Mr. Ackerman to say he's going to be saying the same as Mr. Golic. But we would like a summary. And more importantly, we have no date of birth for this man and we would like the name of his father, and if we could have that please today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do my best to get that to Ms. Korner today, the whole thing. Whatever she wants I'll try to get to her today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we ask, we don't mind whether we have the medical certificates in Serbian and German, so if we could have copies of those today. And while I'm on the question of summaries, Your Honour, for some unknown reason, email doesn't seem to work in the OTP over the weekend, and we've not received a summary for this witness at all. I understand Mr. Cunningham hasn't got a copy here, but that your legal officer may have a copy, and I wonder if we could just have a copy given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. We'll nobody seems to have a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. If my legal assistant had one, she should have given it to us for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. Well, can we take it there is no summary then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I have one at my office on my computer, but I just don't have it with me. And I apologise for that. I don't know what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is three weeks' holiday, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Speak for yourself, Your Honour. With all due respect, I had court all in the States last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What I want to make sure, Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner, is that we can fit in 48 and 49 Friday because -- I don't know. We will need a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if we go beyond the normal hours, we would still need a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. Your Honour, I mean, as I understand it from the short summaries we've got for them, again, we haven't got expanded summaries yet, I think it should be potentially possible to finish both in one day. It may well be that we have to perhaps go beyond the normal court hours. I don't know what the situation is like at the other trials in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was my understanding, Your Honour, that we had reserved Courtroom II for the entire day, not just for the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was my understanding as well. But I see here that we are sitting in Courtroom III, and only the morning session has been reserved. And that in the afternoon, Hadzihasanovic is sitting in the same courtroom. Courtroom II is free in the morning, but there's Strugar in the afternoon. No, sorry, there's Strugar in the morning, but it's free in the afternoon. But I don't know -- I've never done the videolink here, so I don't know whether you can shift from one courtroom to the other. I honestly don't know because there will only be the half an hour break between the first and -- the morning and the afternoon sitting. Or Strugar could move to... Strugar would move to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Strugar move to Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are sitting in the morning in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Strugar, too. Swap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We swap there. See what you can do. I want to make sure that we will be in a position to finalise -- finish these two witnesses on Friday, even if we have -- if we need to sit more than the usual sitting hours. And I'm sure I will find the cooperation of everyone. Can we bring the witness in, or is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There are a couple more matters which really again relate to timetabling. It looks as though the evidence is most likely, other than the expert, Mr. Shoup, is going to finish this week. And as I recall, the expert is going to start testifying on the 9th of February. Your Honour, for the purposes really of now preparation, as it were, have Your Honours over the break finalised any arrangements in respect of any visits you might wish to make to the sites?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'm taking that up with Mr. Roberts today. I just sent him an email first thing this morning to come and see me in the first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Things are moving obviously. And there are two aspects, one is the date, the other one is security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for those -- for security in particular, I have been taught early in my life not to interfere and let others decide for me. As regards the date, I think they are thinking about those, and they will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because Your Honour gave some prospective dates on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Also the tentative schedule that was prepared by Ms. Sutherland and that was given to us, and to Mr. Roberts, and I think he has discussed it with the Registrar, and I think more or less that's what we will be -- that will be more or less the basic schedule, plus or minus obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I can tell Your Honours that the Registrar got in touch with the field office in Banja Luka, and they were going to see, effectively do a test run to see whether it was possible to encompass this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes that was number one. Secondly, because apparently in some areas, I don't know how much weeks' prior notice is needed. So I'm in the hands of others. As soon as we are in a position to suggest dates, then obviously we will come back -- we will come back to you. I will also require to know, Mr. Ackerman, if you finish with the witnesses this week whether you will be available here in The Hague, either of you or both of you, all the time or whether you're going to be in the States on call to come back. I don't know. Please put us in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is more in the hands of the Registry than anyone. If they will permit me to remain here, I will. If they won't, I'll leave. It's pretty much up to them. I think if Your Honour were to suggest on the record or otherwise that you think it's necessary that I remain here, then the Registry would surely permit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I will discuss that with my two colleagues, and eventually with the Registrar if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last matter, again, and it's a question of really timing, is -- it is likely that we will be calling some rebuttal evidence. We're in the process of investigating. But for our purposes and for the time we'll have, are Your Honours able to say at this stage whether at the end of the Defence evidence and any rebuttal evidence we call Your Honours will be seeking to call witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we reserve our decision on that. We discussed it already at some point. But that was before certain events happened. And I think we will have to discuss things again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you that I personally had in mind summoning someone here, but I don't think that is possible now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply -- obviously I'm asking not that I want to put Your Honours on the spot, but because it, of course, makes a difference in terms of the time left for writing the closing submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But taking you up on what you stated possibly will be calling or recalling some witnesses in rebuttal, I don't think that we need -- I mean, to be practical, that we need to wait until Mr. Ackerman's expert witness has come over. If that is the only witness left, I think we could use the time frame between this Friday or Monday coming and the 9th of January when --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: February. Your Honour, that's what I wanted to know because the answer is, Your Honour, we would be -- we would have difficulties. Matters have come to light as it were just before the Christmas break. The Christmas break has meant that it has almost been impossible to conduct, as I'm sure Mr. Ackerman can tell you, any inquiries in Bosnia or the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because everybody is off. Their holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everyone is off for how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They have just come back this week. But therefore, any inquiries we want to make, and there are certain inquiries that we have been trying to make and we are trying to find at least two people, but we haven't been able to get anywhere a request for information delivered to the Bosnian authorities, hasn't yet been responded to, even though it was sent on the 13th of December. So Your Honour, I would ask that the rebuttal remain in the place in which it is, at the end of Mr. Shoup. In any event, we have to give Mr. Ackerman, as he rightly said, notice of any witnesses that we will call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is perfectly in order. But if there is any witness or any witnesses that you could bring over before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously -- there may be one. But there are two in with respect of whom we are still attempting to find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would also put me in a position where I can plead a case with the Registrar to have Mr. Ackerman stay here until... So.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may well be one. I'm going to have a meeting this afternoon in respect of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I rely on your cooperation, as usual. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can bring the witness in and we can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just ask Mr. Cunningham whether -- through Your Honours whether the witness is going to finish in chief today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't got any protective measures, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There's no protective measures, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jokic, and welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence in this trial that has been going on against Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. And in terms of our Rules, you are required to enter a declaration before you start giving evidence, a declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that the usher is handing to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now, yes. We can proceed, I take it that the translation does not change the declaration. The declaration was made by the witness in his own language. So please, take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the effect of the declaration that you have -- solemn declaration that you have made a minute ago is equivalent to that of an oath. In other words, you will be giving testimony, and the solemn declaration applies with regard to all questions irrespective of who is going to put the question to you. You will first be asked questions by Mr. Cunningham who is one of the lawyers defending Mr. Brdjanin, and I suppose you have met him already. He will then be followed by Ms. Korner, who is the leading counsel for the Prosecution in this case. My suggestion to you, my advice to you, is to answer each question as concisely but as fully as possible. Don't give us information that is not asked from you because you will be here for the entire week otherwise. So answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Did I make myself clear? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is any problem with interpretation at any moment, please draw my attention. Thank you. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Zoran Jokic. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your religion is the orthodox religion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what municipality were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which municipality do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been married?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: For 14 -- no, 24 years. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I do. I have two daughters, and I am a proud grandfather, too. I have a grandchild.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Congratulations. Are you now or have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now or have you ever been a member of the communist party, that is, the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Earlier, that is, prior to 1990, I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about your educational background. Did you attend secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend secondary school at?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I attended secondary school in Belgrade. It was a military high school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the completion of your military high school, did you go to university?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I attended air force academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the air force academy in the former Yugoslavia located at?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It was located in Zadar, and it had a department in Pula as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you complete your studies at the air force academy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In 1987, I became a pilot.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because the interpreters had a problem following what you were saying. Could you repeat your answer. The question was: "Did you complete your studies at the air force academy?" And you started saying: "Yes, I did. In 1987, I became a pilot." And then you said something else which the interpreters didn't gather.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said that I had become a pilot in the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says you became a pilot in 1987. Was that a correct translation, or did you become a pilot earlier?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you take your flight training at in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Partly in Zadar and partly in Pula. While I was attending the academy, apart from the theoretical part of the training, we also had practical training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you became a pilot in 1977, did you become a flight instructor where you would teach other individuals to fly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct. After I completed the military academy, I attended specialised courses, various trainings, in order to become a flight instructor. Or as we used to call it, a flight teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you a flight teacher or flight instructor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: For about ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you serve as a flight instructor? Where was the training base or training facility at?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of aircraft did you instruct in? Did you instruct in jet aircraft or other aircraft?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Jet aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you were in the -- and by the way, I'm assuming that after graduating from the air force academy, you entered the Yugoslavian air force. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Yugoslavian air force, did you ever serve as a squadron commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in Banja Luka, sometime in 1991, I became a squadron commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A squadron consists of what? Describe it for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do so. There are pilots who are members of a squadron, but there are also technical staff, officers and noncommissioned officers who maintain and service the aircraft and equip them for flying, and also additional auxiliary staff comprising both officers and noncommissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk about a squadron, roughly speaking how many aircraft are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In a normal formation, that is, in the former JNA, the number of aircraft in an ordinary squadron was between 12 and 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you currently in the air force or in the military now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I have retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you retire -- excuse me for interrupting you, but when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I retired in 1999, sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what rank did you retire with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: With the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now about the command structure in the air force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel, correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the air forces in the former Yugoslavia part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't think one could describe them as such. Air forces are always elite forces within the armed forces of a country. So it was a special part of the Yugoslav People's Army, the air force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before we go on, can I just make it very clear that I'd like this part of the evidence to come without any leading questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a command structure for the Yugoslavian air force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And describe that command structure for this Court, telling us specifically whether it was linked or not linked to the command structure for the army.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Every part of the air force, starting from the lowest ranking unit of the squadron to the larger units, all the way to the command of the air force, had one single line of command. And the air force command had their line of command to the supreme command. The links between the units and the -- there was only one command line between land forces and air forces, and of course the navy. And they were all part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were a squadron commander, who would your immediate supervisor be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: My immediate supervisor would have been the regiment commander, the air force regiment, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If your immediate commander, the regiment commander, gave you an order, were you obligated to follow it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would be above the regiment commander in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In the former JNA, that would have been the corps commander, and then the commander of the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say the corps commander, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the then organisation of the air force; that is, the commander of the air force corps, not the land force corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- okay. And who would then be above the commander of the air force corps in this chain of command you just described?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The chief of general staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the ground forces, as you described it the land forces, how would you describe their chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: From the lowest-ranking land force unit through the higher-ranking units, they had their own command line all the way to the land force corps. From that point on, they were directly responsible to the general staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the commander of a land force corps issue an order to you as a squadron commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Because in the former JNA, and that was probably the case in other countries as well, the line of command was always respected. I had my line of command, and my responsibility went to the commander of the air force regiment and the air force corps, and from there to the commander of the air force and the air force defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What would happen if the commander of a land force corps gave an order to a squadron commander in the air force chain of command? Would that have any effect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. The commander of a land force corps could not issue an order to me as a commander in the air force. If he needed something, I would refer him to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the former JNA, in the air force component of the JNA, was there any civilian that could issue an order to a military officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What impact would there be, if any, if a civilian attempted to order the air force component of the former JNA to take a specific step?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: There was no possibility for a civilian to issue an order to the air force component. There was simply no such possibility. If there were such an attempt, it would obviously be refused. It would not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just told us about the impact, the lack of impact that a civilian order would have on the air force component. Do you know from your 22-odd years in the military the impact if any of a civilian order to other components of the JNA -- do you know what sort of impact, if any, that would have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have talked about the JNA. In the time that you were in the JNA, specifically in 1992, was there a reorganisation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, sometime in mid-1992, the JNA withdrew from the area -- from certain areas of the former Yugoslavia, from Croatia and BH, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did an entity in the former Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina come to replace the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can be direct in this and shorten the list of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is history anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, was the VRS formed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the VRS include a portion of the air force component of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain with the VRS in its air force component after the reorganisation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: For a brief period of time, they were only providing support for this organisation to be -- I was only providing support for this organisation to be completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's make sure that the record is clear. You told us that you retired from the air force sometime in 1999. In 1992, after the reorganisation, were you in the air force component of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. Pursuant to my own request in the summer of 1992, I was transferred to the position of the chief of civilian control at the airfield in Mahovljani [Realtime transcript read in error "^"] on which position I remained until 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that in just a minute, what your duties there entailed. What I'm after, what I want you to discuss is based on your experience after 1992 is to talk about the chain of command within the former VRS -- excuse me, within the VRS, specifically the air force component. You described a chain of command that existed in the JNA. Did that chain of command with respect to the air force component of the VRS, did it change?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't. Well, I cannot claim that it remained the same 100 per cent, but the same chain of command was retained from the JNA. In the Army of Republika Srpska, we respected the same chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the Army of the Republika Srpska, was there a land force component and an air force component?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting with a -- the squadron that you had in 1992, what was the chain of command within the air force component of the VRS? And I'd like for you to tell it to us slowly to make sure that we get the interpretation correct, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The chain of command was as follows: There was a squadron, which was responsible directly to the air force command of the VRS. As to why there were no units in between, it was because the VRS air force was relatively small. So the chain of command went from the squadron to the air force command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a chain of command --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And excuse me, Your Honours. I'm told there's a correction that needs to be noted at line 22, excuse me, page 22, line 5. The witness testified: "I was transferred to the chief of civilian control at the airfield in Mahovljani in 1996." I am told that -- I'm told that he testified that he remained there up until 1996. So if I could get him to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jokic, you were appointed to that position as chief of civilian control at the airfield in Mahovljani when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you remained in that position until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like I said, I don't remember the exact date. But until 1996, and then between 1996 and 1999, I was just an official within the command of the air force before I retired, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm satisfied. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I went into this correction with you, Mr. Jokic, I was about to ask you about the chain of command within the land forces of the VRS. In 1992, were you acquainted or did you know what the chain of command was within the land forces of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was acquainted with the situation. More or less as far as I knew, the similar line of command, the chain of command was kept from the JNA. Lower-ranking units to the corps, and then the corps was responsible to the general staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the commander of the a corps within the VRS issue an order to a squadron commander of the air component of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Because, as I stated earlier, there was a chain of command which we had to respect. That is, I as a squadron commander could only receive orders from my superior air force command. As for the land forces, if they needed air force support, they would have to refer to my superior command, and then my superior command would issue an order to me which I then implemented, or rather the unit of the air force in question would then implement the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What steps, if any, would you take if you as a squadron commander were contacted by a corps commander who was attempting to order you to take a specific step?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I would tell him -- I would refer him to my superior command whose order would then I implement. I'm talking about my unit, the air force unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've talked about the chain of command. What I would like to do now is go back to 1991. In 1991, I believe you told us that you were a flight instructor in the Mostar area. Sometime in 1991, did you get transferred to the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did sometime in late October beginning of November, I don't remember the exact date. In 1991 I arrived in Banja Luka in the airport of Mahovljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you assume a new position or what position if any did you assume upon your arrival in Banja Luka in October/November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I became a squadron commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the squadron was located where?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The squadron was located at the Mahovljani airfield 25 kilometres from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier you described what a squadron consisted of. Was that a fair description of the squadron of the forces that you took command of in October/November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, when I arrived in Banja Luka, this reinforced squadron had a larger number of aircraft and a significant number of technical staff. It had between 20 and 25 aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the reorganisation of the VR -- the reorganisation of the JNA and the birth of the VRS that you've just described, what effect, if any, did that have on the number of aircraft at the squadron's disposal and the number of technical staff at the squadron's disposal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: There was no significant decrease in the number of aircraft. But with the withdrawal of the JNA from the area of the BH, part of the technical staff went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived there in the fall of 1991 to assume command, was there a helicopter detachment in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was a small sports airfield in the area called Zaluzani, and it was there that the helicopter units were stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the helicopter unit, if you will, under your command or was it under someone else's command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, the helicopter units were not under my command. But both helicopter units and my unit, we had a common command. The 5th air force corps during the JNA era which was later reorganised as the 5th operational group of the air force, and it all became part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was there a logistical component to the air force in the area as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was one at the Mahovljani airfield, and also at the Zaluzani airfield to a smaller extent, and they were in charge of providing support to the helicopter units there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you command the logistical component there at the two airfields?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the logistical component, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In the period from the end of 1991 and in early 1992, I remember it was Colonel -- I think it was Lieutenant Colonel first, and then at the end of 1992 he became a colonel. So it was Colonel Biga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Biga a higher ranking officer than you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to your arrival in Banja Luka in October/November of 1991, did you move there with your family?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: We didn't arrive together on the same day. I arrived first, and my wife and my children came to Banja Luka a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you as a family reside on the air force base or did you reside elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. We had an apartment that we rented. Our family rented an apartment in Banja Luka. And we're still living in a rented apartment today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that apartment that you were residing in 1991, 1992, how many kilometres was that from the airfield in Mahovljani?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The apartment was in the centre of town, not the innermost centre, but it was about 25 to 26 kilometres away from the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the airport is located in what municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The Mahovljani airport is in the Municipality of Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took over the command of the forces of the airport near Laktasi, as part of your duties as commander, did you have contact with the civilian authorities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Even in the former JNA, and in the VRS, also there was a rule since the members of the army are -- or people from that area, there was a rule that it was necessary to maintain good relations with the civilian authorities and the people living in that area. We lived together with those people. We were part of those people, so it was important to keep good relations and connections with those people, especially in connection with certain holidays, specific holidays for that region or the holidays of Republika Srpska. We were quite close to the people. They would come to look at our equipment, so we did maintain contacts. I believe that this is quite normal and it is something that is a practice in other parts of the world as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The first time was when I became to Banja Luka, not immediately, but during the first few months of my service in Banja Luka. That's when I met Mr. Radic. And I asked for his help in the allocation of apartments for the pilots because we didn't have any accommodation that was set aside for our pilots and their families in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the first few months of your service in Banja Luka, are you referring to 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say decidedly. Perhaps it was in December. I really don't remember dates very well, so I can't say specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fair enough. And again, what was the purpose of your meeting with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: First of all, to meet him. He was the president of the Banja Luka Municipality at the time. So it was to meet and get to know the president of the municipality because we were living in that area. And perhaps to tell him about our problems, including the housing situation, maybe even in particular about the housing situation, and also to engage him in an informal talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Radic able to provide any help with respect to the housing situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: He promised and for a good part, I think Mr. Radic -- I don't mean Mr. Radic, but the Banja Luka Municipality did help us and did allocate a number of apartments to the members of the air force. But if I may be allowed to mention also, all of these apartments have been returned over the past period so that all of those air force members now are living as tenants. They don't have their own apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With -- when you assumed command of the squadron at the airport near -- in Laktasi Municipality, did you go home to your apartment in Banja Luka every night?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time, let's say December through May, December 1991 through May 1992, describe for this Chamber if you will where you spent the bulk of your time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: When you look at this whole period, I spent most of the time at the Mahovljani airport, most of the time, because I was the commander so I had a lot of things to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you spent most of the time at the airport, on average per week how many nights would you spend at the base?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Four to five definitely, and sometimes the entire week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that during this time period that being the commander you had a lot of things to do. During the time period that I just laid out, December 1991 through May 1992, briefly tell us what sort of things that you had to undertake as the commander.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I've said a little earlier that the unit comprises pilots, technical staff, and soldiers. All of those components had to be commanded. It was necessary to resolve their problems, also problems arising from the maintenance of equipment, the airplanes, looking for components for the machines. So it was necessary to organise the life and the work of the unit in that area, and you know what the conditions were like at the time. It was quite difficult, and it was very difficult to organise all of those things. So there was a lot to do the whole day. So by the time the workday was over, it was quite late so there was no point in returning, and then coming back very early the next morning to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your answer that we knew what the conditions were like at the time. Could you tell us just for the record what the conditions were just so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: During that period, there were clashes in Croatia. The JNA was withdrawing from Croatia and Slovenia. So in the former SFRY, the situation was quite turbulent, so it was normal that this was reflected on the entire life and work, not only of the army but also of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of -- by the rank and name of General Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that man?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: General Ninkovic was the commander of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Ninkovic ever come to Banja Luka to assume command of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came sometime in the month of May. I don't remember whether that was the exact date, but he did come around that time to take over the command, and that's -- after that he was at the head of the air force forces of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon his arrival in Banja Luka, could you describe for the Chamber, for these Judges, what your relationship with him was like?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: General Ninkovic, when he arrived at Banja Luka, told me and his other associates of his vision and plan to form the air force of the Army of Republika Srpska. I did not entirely agree with such a concept. This did not correspond with my view of things. And in all of his conversations, he was offering me posts that did not suit me personally, so I was looking for a way to no longer remain at this post. And I was requesting to be put in a different post. I wanted to be placed, to leave the post that I had, and I wanted to be assigned the post of commander of a flight control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you get along with General Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: We had professional, military relationship which was normal and it was necessary. We were not close outside of our professional soldiers' life. We respected one another as superior officers and officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the answer you just gave us, you described the post you were in. Is that the post as squadron commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the post that you sought?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I've said a little bit before that I was born in the Municipality of Laktasi. To be more specific, the village of Krneta next to Laktasi. And I wanted to stay in that region. I wanted to continue to work in the territory that I was born in. And I thought that the chief of flight control, that that post would be something that would suit me, and I requested to be assigned to that post. And I was permitted, I was assigned to this post eventually. They did take my request into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know you're not perfect with dates. When did you assume the post of the chief of flight control?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: This was sometime in the summer. I think it was in July sometime, but it was definitely sometime during the summer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The airport in Laktasi, was it also -- was it solely reserved for military aircraft?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. The Mahovljani airport in Laktasi was so-called mixed airport, so it serviced both military and civilian aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to do now is I want to go talk to you about whether or not you were involved in flying any combat missions in the spring and summer of 1992. First of all, did you fly any combat missions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In my career generally, is that what you mean? Did I fly any combat missions in the course of my career?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that you were listening very carefully. I really wanted to know whether in the spring and summer of 1992 you were flying any combat missions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did fly a number of combat missions, combat flights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fly any combat missions over Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fly any combat missions to deal with the resistance in Kotor Varos municipality, specifically in the area or the village or the hamlets of Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time period that we're talking about, specifically the spring and summer of 1992, what was the fuel or petrol situation like with respect to the squadron at the airport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: We did not have sufficient quantities of fuel in the former JNA -- I'm talking -- in comparison to the situation in the early 1980s. Then we didn't have a problem with fuel. During the period you mentioned, during that period we did have to take care about the quantities of fuel that we had, and we had to use these quantities of fuel in a rational way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the blockade affect your ability to get sufficient supplies of petrol, jet fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't doubt the fact that it did have some effect on it. I have no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you acquainted with the munitions that were typically carried by aircraft in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of 1992, certain combat missions which I participated in usually used artillery or gun cannon munitions. They also had bombs, classic bombs, as well as rocket munition. But smaller rocket munitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these munitions you've just described include chemical weapons or chemical components?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The munitions that we had, that we carried, no. I have not even heard of us even having chemical munitions or chemical weapons. I've never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After assuming the command of the squadron in September/November 1991, did you meet General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The previous commander from whom I took over my duty, of course, introduced me to certain structures within the army and those within -- the authorities within the municipalities of Laktasi and Banja Luka. And of course, I met those people. And if I can remember correctly, I met General Talic at the JNA hall, the army hall. We had a brief introductory conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, recognising that you can't remember a specific date, would you be kind enough to tell us roughly speaking when that was, that you met General Talic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Sometime before the new year in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did that meeting with General Talic last?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It was very brief. Perhaps for about half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly for us to get to know one another, for Mr. Talic to meet me as the new commander of the aviation unit and for me to meet General Talic at the time he was in the 1st Krajina Corps. That was still called the 5th Krajina Corps at the time. Later it was called the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between this first meeting in late 1991 and the end of 1992, did you have any additional face-to-face, personal meetings with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Personal meetings between the two of us did not take place, but I did see Mr. Talic in passing. However, there were no personal meetings or encounters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the time that you assumed command of the aviation component at the airport until the end of 1992, did General Talic in his capacity as corps commander or in any other capacity issue you an order to take specific steps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Not to me personally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of him issuing an order to any other air force officer during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've talked about some of the events in Banja Luka in 1991. I want to take you to April of 1992. In April of 1992, how did you get from Banja Luka, where your family lived, to the airport? Did you have a private vehicle or did you have a military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Most of the time I used a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this probably is a silly question to a former air force officer. When you went to work, did you go in civilian clothes or did you go in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a uniform was compulsory. So for -- in 1990 and 1991, but as well as for 90 per cent of my life I have been wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In early 1992, did you become aware of the Serbian Defence Forces in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of them? Did you -- I'll let you answer it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: At a checkpoint, at a control point which was organised by those forces towards the airport, I was stopped there on my way to the airport. They introduced themselves. When they saw that I was an officer, there were no problems, and I continued to my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe for the Chamber, if you will, how these individuals were dressed, if they were in uniform or civilian clothes, and whether they were armed or unarmed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms just like all the other members of the land force units, and they were armed. I cannot remember exactly now what kind of weapons they had, but they did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wear any distinctive headgear or have any distinctive insignia on their shoulder?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice the insignia. I think that they were wearing caps or a kind of smaller type of headgear or a hat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your initial reaction when you saw these armed, camouflaged -- armed troops wearing camouflage uniforms stopping your military vehicle? Who did you think they were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I thought that they were members of one of the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, which was in that area. This was the territory of the 1st Krajina Corps, so I thought in accordance with someone's decision they were instructed to set up these checkpoints. I didn't think anything unusual in them manning the checkpoints or setting up the checkpoints, and I wasn't surprised or thought it was very unusual in any way that I was stopped. I didn't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you find out that they were not assigned to or affiliated with the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In a later period. A while had gone by before I found out that they were not affiliated or that they were not members of any of the 1st Krajina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm at a good breaking point if this is a convenient point for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It certainly is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Strictly, Your Honour, I think it's the 5th Krajina Corps at this stage, just to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a short break of 25 minutes, and we will resume immediately after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we continue, firstly as Your Honours will see, Mr. Nicholls has now joined us in court fresh from his holiday. Second, this: Your Honour, it may be because this is starting back again after the new year, but I'm told that again, what is said here is being broadcast outside the hours. What was being said in court before Your Honours came in and before official broadcasting started was being transmitted to televisions within the building. Your Honour, I think it may be just a glitch because this is the first case back after the new year, but can I just mention it again because it's obviously important that only the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's very important.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had the same thing happening before the Christmas recess, and that is very unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the difficulties of course is that conversations go on between counsel in order to assist with administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is not something that need and should be in our submission broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner. And may I draw your attention to this, Madam Registrar, and you will liaise with whoever is responsible for this. I think what's done cannot be undone today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But all precautions should be taken to avoid this happening again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just very briefly, on the topic of being able to call rebuttal evidence, Your Honour, during the break I received notification again that apparently, which I had forgotten, it's the new year in the Republika Srpska tomorrow, and so it doesn't appear that anybody's working today either. So we're having real difficulty in pursuing our inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But -- I understand that, Ms. Korner, and I leave this in your hands. I know that you will do your level best to cooperate. So I have no reason to complain. The witness is here. Mr. Cunningham, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, I forgot to ask a question, so I'll apologise to you and the Chamber and to opposing counsel because it's a little bit out of order. You told us that you were transferred from the Mostar area to Banja Luka October/November of 1991. Did the remainder of the JNA air forces in that region get transferred as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the part of the forces that were transferred from Mostar to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. It was only me personally who was transferred from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During the time period that you assumed the command, October/November 1991, up through the end of the year of 1992 did you read newspapers on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow TV?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: When I had the opportunity of doing so, yes. But the most quality broadcast was from the Croatian television at the Mahovljani airfield because that's the area very near to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is it that you -- could you receive any TV transmissions from the Banja Luka area while you were at the airport? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could receive Banja Luka TV programmes, but with frequent interruptions and irregular broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what caused the frequent interruptions and irregular broadcasting schedule?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really answer your question, but I believe it was technical problems and less than perfect functioning of the TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect if any did your job obligations first as squadron commander and then as chief of flight or air control, how did that affect your ability to follow TV news and TV broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: While I was a squadron commander, I did not have enough time to watch TV. As for the free time that I would have from time to time during the day, I used that opportunity to relax a little bit, to do some sports to the extent it was possible because, of course, it was also our obligation to remain fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that as part of your obligations as squadron commander, you would make contact with the civilian structures. You told us about your meeting with Mr. Radic with respect to housing for the pilots. In your liaising, contacting the local civilian structures when you assumed command, did you have any contact with Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, not during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you have your first contact with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting of the AR Krajina that I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the AR Krajina," are you talking about the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm referring to the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you to bring a notebook that I provided you with earlier that had several copies of public exhibits as well as your statement. What I'd like for you to do is get that at the ready because I'm going to ask you to look at a document. Were you a member of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you got that position? Did you volunteer for it? Did you apply for it? How is it that you got it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I was informed by a friend of mine who came to my office together with the late Mr. Slobodan Dubocanin, and they explained to me that I had been elected to become a member of the AR Krajina as a representative of the air force. They asked me whether I would be willing to become a member, and in view of the fact that I lived in the area, that I was part of that community, I thought it was my obligation to cooperate with the civilian authorities. And I didn't see at that point in time anything wrong with my becoming a member. So I agreed, and he told me that he would inform me of the next meeting or that someone would inform me of the next meeting which was to take place in Banja Luka. And he told me that I should attend this meeting if, in view of my other obligations, that was possible. So I agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the exhibit -- in that book right there, there should be a tab, and I believe it says "168" on it. If you could go to the tab, I want you to look at that document, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a document dated 5 May 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A decision listing who are the members of the ARK Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until this point, this point being 5 May 1992, had you met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your daily activities within the municipalities of Banja Luka and Laktasi, had you ever heard of Mr. Brdjanin at this point? Again, 5 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I can tell you specifically whether I've ever heard. I may have, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you tell us that you were informed of this by a friend who accompanied by Slobodan Dubocanin came out to the airport and told you about the ARK Crisis Staff and asked if you would be amenable to serve on it. Did they explain to you anything about what purpose the crisis staff would serve?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, they did not. I was simply told that this would be discussed at the meeting that I was supposed to attend, that we would see together what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we were to look again at Exhibit P168, we see among the 17 or so entries, we'll see the name of Predrag Radic. You've told us that you had met Mr. Radic with respect to liaising with the community and discussing housing with the -- Mr. Radic. Looking at that list, prior to 5 May 1992, the date of that document, did you know, personally know, any of the other individuals listed in Exhibit P168?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Prior to 5th of May, no. I said I had met Slobodan Dubocanin, and I knew only superficially Nenad Stevandic through my friends. I had met him, but we didn't really socialise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's follow up on what you just said. When did you first meet Slobodan Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember the exact date. It was a long time ago. But I know that it was, once again, through our mutual friends since I arrived in Banja Luka only in October or November 1991. I had some friends there, people whom I had known from before, and it was those friends who introduced me to Dubocanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Dubocanin prior to your arrival in October/November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you knew only -- that you knew Mr. Nenad Stevandic only superficially through your friends. Did you know Mr. Stevandic or know of Mr. Stevandic prior to your arrival in October/November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it between October/November 1991 and the date of that document in front of you, P168, dated 5 May 1992, how is it that you came to know Mr. Stevandic superficially?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: We had mutual friends. Some of my friends and acquaintances were also his friends, and that is how we met. But it was only very briefly because I rarely ventured downtown. And it was only later that I really met him, and that I realised that I had already seen him a couple of very brief occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- when you talk about these superficial meetings or knowing him, Mr. Stevandic, only superficially through friends, give us some sort of idea what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: What I talked about him? Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a bad question on my part. Let me rephrase it. You said that you knew him only superficially. How long did you -- were you in the company of Mr. Stevandic when you met him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: For about 15 or 20 minutes briefly. Those were chance encounters. I would run into him when I was with some friends of mine. But once again, they were very brief encounters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of these very brief encounters do you recollect having with Mr. Stevandic prior to 5 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact number, but there were very few such encounters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the very few brief encounters you had with Mr. Stevandic, was there anything of substance discussed with respect to politics, the current security situation, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, those were once again accidental, chance encounters. We had not agreed to meet. So we would just talk informally. He was always interested in pilots, and he seemed to have been glad to know a pilot. Those were very informal meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that when your friend and Slobodan Dubocanin came to you and asked if you were interested in serving on the ARK Crisis Staff, you told us that there was going to be a meeting. Did you attend meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: When I was informed by telephone that a meeting would take place, I don't know whether that was the first meeting of the crisis staff to take place, but I was invited to attend it. And they informed me a day before, so they said that the next day a meeting would take place, and I attended it the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see Exhibit P168 again dated 5 May 1992 again as the benchmark or starting point, do you have a recollection of when the first meeting you attended was? Was it on the 5th of May, or do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How many meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff did you attend? What is your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I didn't keep a precise record, but I believe I attended four or five meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you notified by a telephone call when the crisis staff was meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was usually the case. By telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption. Were you ever notified of a meeting but failed to attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was it that you as an air force pilot during this time period did not attend meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I had my formal obligations, my commitments as a soldier which I deemed to be more important. And physically it was impossible for me to be at two locations at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could not attend a meeting, would you send a representative from the squadron or from the air force in your place instead?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
