utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you attended four or five meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff. When you did attend, how long would you stay?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I would usually stay for as long as it lasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did there come a time when you just ceased to go to ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what prompted your decision to stop attending?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Personally I believed that I was not indispensable, that my presence was not necessary, simply because all of the decisions and generally speaking the discussions were not related to the air force, and that is why I believe that my presence was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that there would be times when you would be notified of a meeting, and because of other obligations you didn't attend. In those situations when you were notified and didn't attend, did anyone ever call you, write you, contact you and protest the fact that you were absent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those situations where you were notified but didn't attend because of other obligations, were there ever any sanctions or punishment for your failure to attend?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I was an officer. And in no case could the crisis staff undertake any sanctions with respect to me due to failure to attend. The crisis staff was a civilian structure after all, and I was a military officer who respected his military duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, perhaps I would like to interrupt you -- interrupt here. Perhaps you could ask him two questions related to this one. First, whether -- when he failed to attend or when he decided not to attend any of the meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff, whether he sent a substitute? But I want that clear. And secondly is whether he reported to his immediate superiors his decision not to attend or his not attending in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'll just adopt your questions because they were phrased expertly and ask him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, when you failed to attend or when you decided not to attend, did you ever send a substitute?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, nor did I have a substitute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you attended meetings and upon return to the base, did you report to General Ninkovic or anyone in the air force chain of command what had happened at the ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. After all, I didn't have an obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say you didn't have an obligation to do so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No one had imposed such an obligation on me, so it was my understanding that I was not under any obligation to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you deal in -- through May and June -- May, June, and July of 1992, how often would you see General Ninkovic or speak with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that we saw each other frequently because General Ninkovic spent most of his time in Banja Luka, and I spent most of my time at the Mahovljani airfield. But we did speak and we would see each other from time to time with respect to technical problems, organisational problems regarding the air force. Mainly technical, professional aspects of our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would speak with him and see him on those occasions, did he, General Ninkovic, ever express any interest whatsoever in the crisis staff and the proceedings of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Obviously, he knew I was a member of the crisis staff. But he never asked too many questions about the crisis staff, so it is my opinion that he discussed these issues with someone else. But again, I'm not sure. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that there came a time when you decided that you were not indispensable to the crisis staff, the ARK Crisis Staff, and ceased to attend. If the first meeting of the crisis staff was on or about May 5th, 1992, what is your recollection of when you quit going?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I quit attending those meetings after a month or month and a half. At that time, the air force command had already started operating, and General Ninkovic had more contacts with the representatives of the town and representatives of some other organisations that were located in the town. And I would not be present. I was already getting ready to take over my new position, and it was my personal decision that it was no longer necessary for me to attend those meetings because I was already in this transitional period of handing over my duty as a commander. I was no longer so active within the air force, and I believe that there were other individuals that were more capable of doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you stopped attending after the month, month and a half you just described, did anyone associated with the ARK Crisis Staff or the Autonomous Region of Krajina ever call you up, contact you to find out where you went and why you stopped coming?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: None did so officially. No one told me officially or formally. But when I took over my duty, I had more time left, and I started seeing my friends more often, and I started going to town more frequently. But it didn't seem like a big thing. I mean, the fact that I had stopped attending those meetings and that practically speaking I was no longer their member, no one thought it to be a major issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that none did so officially. Were there any unofficial contacts with people directing you to return to the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no one suggested to me that I should go back to the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that when you were notified of a meeting and failed to attend because of other obligations, there were no punishments handed out to you. When you flat out stopped going, were there any sanctions, any punishments given to you for your -- for ceasing to serve as a member of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, there were no sanctions or pressure whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the four or five meetings that you attended in the month, month and a half after May 5, 1992, did you ever see anyone from the government in Pale attend meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meetings that you attended, did you ever see anyone that attended the meetings that came from Belgrade or was affiliated with the government structures in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the exhibit again, I think it's P168, that has the listing of the people that were appointed to the ARK Crisis Staff, when you attended your first meeting how many of those 15 individuals, I believe it is, were in attendance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count them, but I think that there were about ten people present. At the time, I didn't think I was obliged to count them or see exactly who was there. But I think that there were about ten people present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the four or five meetings you attended, what would be the head count? How many individuals would be at these four or five meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Each meeting had about that average, except for one meeting which was extended. There were more people present. Usually, there would be between 10 to 12 people present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you talked about a -- one meeting that was extended. How many people roughly speaking were at this extended meeting that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact number again, but in my estimate there were about 40 to 50 people. But do not take this as a precise figure, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the meetings that were attended by 10 to 12 people, generally speaking were those people, individuals reflected in the exhibit in front of you, P168, the document dated 5 May?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of 168?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less those people were present because later I met them, so I knew that it was them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at Exhibit P168, I know at the time that you were appointed to the ARK Crisis Staff you didn't know these individuals, except maybe one or two. But in the time you served on the ARK Crisis Staff, did you come to find out what municipality these 15 individuals were from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know where each of those 15 people were from, from which municipalities. But I found out that more or less most of them were from the Banja Luka area. But I didn't know where each one of them was from because I didn't know each person individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the four or five meetings that you attended, at those meetings did you ever see General Talic there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When General Talic was not in attendance or could not attend, was there anyone representing the interests of the army in attendance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: That's right. The meetings that I attended were also attended by Colonel, and I found out his name later so I can say it now. It was Colonel Vojinovic or Vujinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role if any did Colonel Vujinovic play at these meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff? Was he an active participant in discussions? Describe it for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I've said that I didn't know him. I personally thought that he was a representative of the Krajina Corps, a representative of the land forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at these meetings, what would Colonel Vujinovic do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember now. I know that he sat there, and if somebody asked a question he would respond to that question. But he didn't do anything in particular which would be memorable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or come to know Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the times that you were in attendance, did you see him attend meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: He didn't attend all of them, but I do recall seeing him at crisis staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he failed to attend, did you see anyone who appeared to be a representative of the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that there was a police representative in police uniform, but I didn't know that man or those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about representatives from the army and representatives from the police. In the times that you attended, did you see the ARK Crisis Staff or Mr. Brdjanin ever attempt to issue a direct order to either the military structures or the civilian security structures?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: When I attended the meetings, no one, and Mr. Brdjanin in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particular, did not ever issue any orders, especially to the military structures. And as far as I recall, neither to the representatives of the police structures. Mr. Brdjanin never issued an order to the military representatives. And as I said a little bit earlier, he wasn't able to do that either because I was an officer who respected the chain of command. And I did not wish to deviate from that for a single moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What impact, if any, would an order of the ARK Crisis Staff have on a member of the former JNA or the VRS in light of the chain of command that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we establish the basis, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For that question. In other words --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In other words, on what basis can he venture this opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in the military --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. This is the ARK Crisis Staff established in May of 1992. So for these purposes, however long he was in the military is not relevant. I want to know on what basis he's able -- he may well be able to, but I need to know the basis first, that he's able to say that this particular structure could not issue orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the ARK Crisis Staff a recognised entity in the chain of command of the former JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Not in any case. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of that, what effect, if any, would an order from the ARK Crisis Staff have on the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: First, simply an order could not be issued. I explained this earlier. And had there been an attempt to issue any order, then such an order would not be carried out. I am talking about the members of the military now, especially the units I was a part of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about your liaison with Mr. Radic with respect to housing. Do you remember seeing Mr. Radic in attendance at any meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I think that he did attend one, and not even a whole meeting. He was there just briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to speak with Mr. Radic while you were on the ARK Crisis Staff about Mr. Radic's perceptions, his thoughts about the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukic, did you ever see him in attendance at the four or five meetings that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I think that he did attend. I can't tell you how many, but he did attend them. I did see him at meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us of your superficial relationship with Mr. Stevandic prior to the ARK Crisis Staff. What was his attendance record like with respect to the four or five meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: He was not present each time I attended them. But I can say that he was present a couple of times when I was there. But for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What about Mr. Brdjanin? At the four or five meetings you attended, was he present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I think that he did attend all of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting with the first meeting, if you can, can you recall what role Mr. Brdjanin played at the first meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was the first meeting of the crisis staff or not, but I think that it wasn't. But when I attended that meeting, Mr. Brdjanin was presiding over the meeting. He was sitting at the head of the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not anyone was taking notes or taking the minutes of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I remember that a person called Boro was sitting next to him, and that he was taking the minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever -- after attending a meeting or prior to attending a meeting, were you given copies of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I personally was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm focussing only on these meetings that averaged ten or so people in it. At these meetings, do you recall the focus of the discussion? Specifically, what municipality or municipalities were the focus of the discussions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: When I attended them, the topic was mostly the Municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I assumed that it was so because Banja Luka was the centre generally before of Bosanska Krajina, and then later of Krajina, and now it is the centre of Republika Srpska. And probably it had the most of the problems, and there was a need to discuss these problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about some of these issues, some of these problems, at these meetings - and I'm talking about the smaller meetings now; I'll get to the larger meeting that you attended in a bit - but in the smaller meetings, was there ever any discussion of personnel policy or employment policy with respect to companies within the Banja Luka Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say anything about the employment policy, but there was discussion that key posts in key enterprises should have people there who were loyal to the Republika Srpska at the time. So that it was necessary to make sure that loyal people occupied the management positions in some of these sensitive companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military officer, what do you mean when you talk about "key posts in key enterprises"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I think that key positions are the position of director, deputy director. This is my personal opinion. I am not really versed in that as a professional military person. I'm not well versed in the civilian structures, but I think a key post in a civilian enterprise is the post of a director, and key enterprises would be -- or companies would be those who are of major importance for a certain region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would key enterprises have a security component in a time of war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really respond specifically or precisely to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. You told us that there were discussions about directors, associate directors, and the like. What was being suggested at the ARK Crisis Staff meetings that you attended with respect to these directors in key enterprises?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No conclusions or any particular decisions were made, at least at the meetings that I attended. I don't recall them being taken. But this discussion took part to the effect that loyal citizens of Republika Srpska and those who were loyal to the leadership should be placed at leadership positions at these significant enterprises or institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, what would happen to the individuals who would be by necessity removed when those loyal to the leadership took over the leadership positions in these enterprises?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot really discuss this question. I wasn't a part of those town structures, so I don't know exactly what happened with those people, especially in that period when I didn't really spend that much time in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were on the crisis staff and attended the smaller meetings, was there ever any discussion with respect to the removal of non-Serbs from positions in the military?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I think that those meetings, the official meetings, nobody ever put questions like that during such meetings. Explicit requests by the AR Krajina Crisis Staff were not made, at least not to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At least for part of the time that you were on the ARK Crisis Staff, you were the squadron commander at the airport. Did you have any non-Serbs in your command or under your command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any non-Serb pilots, part of which you called the elite forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my deputy was a Croat, and the commander of the department, which is a lower formation, was a Muslim. And besides the two of them, there were other Muslims and Croats. There was even a Hungarian person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these individuals that you've just described in your answer remain in the -- first the JNA, then as it evolved into the VRS, did they remain in those entities through the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: My deputy, with the withdrawal of the JNA, the deputy, the Croat deputy that I mentioned, so with the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. His post was taken by another Croat. And the commander of the squad whom I mentioned, Muslim, was one of the Muslims who was in the unit. And through unfortunate circumstances with another colleague, he was actually killed during a test flight. This was due to a technical fault. There were two of them on the test flight, him and another Serb. So this was not -- they were not killed during a combat flight, but just during a technical check of the airplane.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because the interpretation is still going on. Could I ask you to repeat, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 58, line 4, did you ever blank any non-Serb pilots? I think the question was did you ever have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I could agree to that straightaway without referring the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, I want to get back on line with the topics that were discussed or not discussed at the crisis staff meetings that you attended. At any of the meetings you attended, was there any discussion of camps, specifically the camps at Omarska, Manjaca, and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, not at the meetings I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of the actual conditions at Omarska, at Manjaca, and at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: When the war ended, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you become aware of Omarska, Manjaca, and Keraterm? Let me put it this way: As a military officer, would you have known of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The Manjaca region and the military units that were up there was something that I knew about. But there was a tank unit there. It was a tank operation centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cunningham, because I think we need to clarify this. Your question referred or addressed the witness's possible knowledge or awareness of the existence of Manjaca. Are you restricting or limiting yourself only to Manjaca as a military --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you were referring -- you mean by putting the question to ask the witness whether he was aware at the time or at some later time of the existence of Manjaca as a collection centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Or as a camp for the detention of several persons there, I think you need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely. But I wanted to establish the fact, I believe, that he would have known of Manjaca as a training facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I took it that you were putting that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm getting there. I wanted to go step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if I could just lead on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military officer, you were aware of the training facility, the tank training facility at Manjaca. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about it back from 1977 when I became an officer. This was a permanent centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, 1992 were you aware that this facility at Manjaca was used as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In 1991, no. In the beginning of 1992, even in the initial phases when I was still the -- a member of the crisis staff, no. I found out about it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say later, how much later are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: A few months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you found out about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how I found out about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, were you aware that the facilities at Omarska mines and at the Keraterm plant were used as detention or collection centres for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I just want to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become aware that these two facilities were used for detention centres or collection centres for the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, the evidence is they weren't used as collection centres in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If it's a question of semantics --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not semantics, it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner's intervention is in place. If there is nothing to indicate that these two places, centres, were used for that purpose in 1991, there's no point in asking him when he became aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's fair. I'll just move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were on the crisis staff and attended these smaller meetings, was there ever any discussion that you recall with respect to the relocation of the non-Serb population within the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. Not at the meetings that I attended, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, your answer suggests that there was some discussion outside the meetings. Were you aware of any discussions outside these meetings about the relocation of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not aware of any such conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the meetings you attended, was there any concern ever raised about the presence of paramilitaries within the territory of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, concern was expressed about the existence of such forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we talk about such forces, which ethnicities -- paramilitaries of which ethnicity were the concern of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood at the time, I think the crisis staff was concerned about the paramilitary formations of any ethnicity. At such meetings, the possibility of one ethnic group having paramilitary forces and another not was not permitted. Generally, the concern was about the existence of any paramilitary forces, if we can say it like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically were there discussions while you were present about -- where people, individuals of the crisis staff expressed concerns about the presence of Serbian paramilitaries within the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is about as leading a question on a topic that Mr. Cunningham well knows --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think a leading objection is sufficient. I get the point, and I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's too late. Your Honour, I really do object to that. Mr. Cunningham knows fully that this is an issue that has been debated over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, again, if it's too late, there's nothing to do to remedy the situation except --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Except to warn Mr. Cunningham this is coming close to contempt of Your Honours' rulings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase the question, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is the practice we have adopted here is that you all know what the Rules are, and we are all closing a blind eye most of the time because most of the time there are leading questions, and we intervene when there is an objection. So it's always walking a tight-- on a tightrope in this area. And I suppose the only thing we can do at this point in time --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but it's pretty late in the case. Your Honour, may I finish, there's very few witnesses left to come and none that will deal with this topic. But Your Honour knows and Mr. Cunningham knows, and this is deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You know, Judge, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He had put the question and phrased it differently a minute, a minute and a half ago. But anyway, let's not waste more time on this. Mr. Cunningham, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'll just move to a new area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour. Leading it may be, but let's hear what the witness has to say about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, do you even remember what the question is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you that he does, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember the question, would you be kind enough to give us an answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand the phrasing of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you rephrase it now, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'm just going to move on to another topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to direct your attention to the one meeting you attended where you thought that perhaps there were somewhere between 40 to 50 people at the meeting. Do you remember when that meeting you attended -- this larger meeting, do you remember when that was in the month or month and a half that you were on the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the date because I didn't keep any record whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you remember whether it was towards the beginning of your time on the crisis staff; that is, around the first part of May, or whether it was towards the end of your time on the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the midterm of my -- in the middle of my attendance as a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Remembering the individuals who are listed on the Exhibit 168 in front of you, were any of those individuals at this meeting, the larger meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the majority were present. The majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember who else was in attendance other than the individuals you just alluded to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the present were the representatives of the Krajina municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any specific recollection of any of these representatives of the municipality? Do you remember any specific people that were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I remember that the meeting was attended by the representative of the Prijedor Municipality, the late -- a police officer. I cannot remember his name. And the president of the municipality of Prijedor, Mr. Stakic, at the time. Oh yes, I remember it was late Mr. Simo Drljaca who was representing the Prijedor Municipality as well. I didn't know other representatives of the municipalities, nor did I meet them later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Brdjanin at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did he play at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was sitting at the head of the table, so I assume that he chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want you to assume. What is your recollection of what role, if any, he played at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you recall happening or being the subject or topic of discussion at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The topic of discussion at the meeting, as far as I can remember, it was a long time ago, revolved mostly around the economic situation in the municipalities and the ways to ensure adequate supply of the municipalities with fuel and various things that were lacking, also about how to ensure proper work of the institutions and so on and so forth. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discussion was mainly about the life and work in general in the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us what you mean when they're talking about the economic situation. What are -- are the representatives from the municipalities addressing or speaking to the gathered group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the representatives from the municipalities requested certain amounts of fuel and other staples which were lacking in those faraway municipalities, the municipalities that were at some distance from Banja Luka and where supply was difficult. So it was mainly about these issues and how to organise life in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what response if any did Mr. Brdjanin have to these representatives requesting fuel and staples and how to organise? Did he have a response?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: To my recollection, he expressed his concern about the difficult circumstances in those municipalities. I didn't believe that he could provide that. I didn't think that he was omnipotent, but I believed in his efforts to provide those municipalities with what they needed in the most efficient and quality way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Ms. Korner. Cross-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a JNA officer you were obliged to keep, weren't you, a workbook?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which you would record the meetings which you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. What's the difficulty about my question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: What meetings which I attended? And in respect of which I was obliged to keep notes do you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were obliged, you just agreed with me, to keep a workbook as a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that workbook, you recorded, did you not, your daily movements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your tasks which had been allocated to you by your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tasks which you allocated to your junior officers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Not all of the tasks. I was not duty-bound to record all of the tasks that I issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And meetings that you had that were concerned or were a part of your duties as a military - and by that I mean air force officer? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have to record any meetings that you had that were part of your professional duties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Now I should tell you about the organisation that we had. I had an assistant, and he had a special --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think you answer the question that was put to you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you can tell me about the organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you telling us, sir, that you didn't have to record any meetings that were held as part of your professional duties which you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I really don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try and put it one more time in the simplest possible terms. If you were called to attend a meeting with General Ninkovic with, let's say, a representative of the 1st Krajina Corps, would you make a note first that you had to attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: All of the meetings that I had with Mr. Ninkovic were recorded by me. I was never invited to any meeting at the Krajina Corps. And outside my professional duties, no, such meetings were never recorded in that notebook. I was only obliged to record the things that were related to me as an officer, as the commander. The things that had something to do with the military. Outside the military structure and apart from the military meetings, no, I was under no obligation whatsoever to keep any official record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was, Mr. Jokic, a very simple, straightforward question. We've now gone around the houses for the last three minutes. Is the answer to my question that yes, you were obliged to record in your workbook meetings that you held as part -- or that you attended as part of your professional duties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it take you so long to answer that very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question as being argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. The Trial Chamber will draw its conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those meetings that you attended of the ARK Crisis Staff were part of your function as a military officer, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to understand what you're saying. Are you saying that effectively you attended those meetings in your personal capacity as a, by then, Squadron Leader Jokic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I attended those meetings on behalf of the air force, as a member of the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were there in your professional capacity as a member of the air force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was a member of the air force. So of course I attended the meeting as a member of the air force. I couldn't attend it in any other capacity. Throughout that time, I was a member of the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these meetings were something that you should have recorded in your workbook, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I had not been ordered by anyone or requested by anyone to keep a notebook regarding those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your workbook was something that could be called for at any time, couldn't it, by your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, that was not a rule in our service. Only the workbook, the notebook, which was kept by my assistant. That was the diary that the superior officers could peruse. As for my personal notebook, that was my own thing, my personal thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But it wasn't your personal thing to do with as you wanted, was it? It was an official record of your movements, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It was my workbook. It contained my tasks, my movements, preparations for other tasks, other things, a notebook where I kept a record of my overall activity. I noted in that notebook whatever I thought was important or necessary, and I used this workbook later on to transfer some information to the official book because I cannot remember everything. And it was a kind of aide memoire as to what I had to do, what I had to accomplish. If anyone requested anything of me, I could use this notebook to refresh my memory. But this was different from the official book which was kept by my assistant. I had my own workbook, and I would use it as an aide memoire in meetings with other commanders, officers, to refresh my memory. It was a simple workbook of an officer which did not constitute an official document of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to try and understand this, please. Are you saying that the workbook that you are referring to was your own personal, if you like, diary and was not a document that was required under your rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, this little red notebook was not an official document of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your account is, is it, that you as an officer didn't have to keep your own official notebook; there was just an official notebook of the unit? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the interpretation. If I understand your question correctly, that notebook was not the official notebook of the unit. There was another one which was the official notebook. But that one was not an official one. It was my personal notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're back to where we started. Leave aside the official record of the unit's activities, were you as a serving officer in the JNA - and I'll come on to the VRS in a moment - obliged to keep an official notebook which recorded your activities and movements? You personally, your own notebook?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Had the obligation to keep it. I mean, I had the obligation to possess such a notebook and to keep record, but it was my document. It belonged to me. It was my personal notebook from which I could collect information from previous periods for the purposes of future purposes and so on and so forth. It was my personal notebook, and that was the case-- that was how we worked. But the official notebook was a different thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unit's -- I accept there was an official notebook for the unit. But your notebook could have been called for, couldn't it, by your superiors at any stage if they wanted to check on what you'd been doing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: That never happened. The officials, if they wanted to know something, they would ask me a question. They wanted me to tell them that. Not a single time in my career as a military officer did anyone ask me to produce this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was not the question that was put to you, Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Jokic. Now listen very carefully. If there had been a matter about which the superiors of an officer wished to make inquiry, for example, involving a disciplinary matter, that notebook kept by that officer could be examined, could it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, it was important for the officer to keep a record of what he was doing and where he was at any given time. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I could accept that as being correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if anybody had made an inquiry as to where you were for some hours on a particular day when you were attending a crisis staff meeting, are you really telling us there would have been no record in your official notebook?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: There would have been a record on a meeting that I had, for instance, the time, 12.00, meeting of the crisis staff. There would have been such an entry indicating my obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Then why did you tell us and tell Mr. Cunningham some minutes ago that you never kept a record of the meetings that you attended of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I thought that the question concerned the contents of the meetings, as to what had happened at the meetings. This notebook of mine contained the schedule of my obligations, so I thought that the question referred to the topics of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you were asked about dates, and you said you kept no records. Now, you could have, couldn't you? You could give us every date on which you attended an ARK Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't state the dates because I destroyed all of them, all of those notebooks and records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, because when the war ended, I didn't think it was necessary to keep it. I wanted to forget the war and everything as soon as possible. And it was a kind of also burden to keep it. I'm not a historian. I didn't have any intention whatsoever to write a book. I didn't think it was necessary for me to have it. I no longer needed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think you'd taken part in activities, either in the course of your military duties or these attendances of the crisis staff meetings, which might be construed as criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this point I have no option. Mr. Jokic, it is the Rule -- one of the Rules of this Tribunal establishes in the same context an obligation that I, as Presiding Judge, have vis-a-vis a witness who is testifying in these proceedings. And what I am going to tell you now is provided for in our Rules by way of protection of the witness. In terms of our Rules, if you are asked a question which if you answer could expose you to criminal proceedings, could incriminate you, in other words, then you can ask us, me and the other two Judges, to be exempted from answering that question. We can say yes or we can say no. We can exempt you from answering the question. We can ask you to answer the question. If we ask you to answer the question, then I also need to explain to you that whatever you say here cannot be used as evidence against you, either before this Tribunal or elsewhere. Ms. Korner has put to you a question, and I will repeat it. I think I have to go into this first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's on the screen still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, it is. The question was: "Do you think you'd taken part in activities, either in the course of your military duties or these attendances of the crisis staff meetings, which might be construed as criminal offences?" I think this is the kind of question which if it causes you this concern that I referred to you before, you can ask us to be exempted from answering. If you feel you can answer that question without exposing yourself to any criminal proceedings or incrimination, then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was not aware of the Rules that you have just apprised me of, and I should ask the permission not to answer this question. I simply didn't know that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- That it would affect me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to take it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the decision of the Trial Chamber is to accede to your request, Mr. Jokic. You are exempted from answering this question. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's probably a suitable time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I want to address the Chamber outside the witness's presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are going to have a short break again of 25 minutes to give you a chance to have a coffee and take a coffee ourselves. Please escort the witness out. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I asked that the witness could be withdrawn so there could be no suggestion that I'm trying to telegraph an answer to the witness. With all due respect, I don't think the witness understood your admonition. I think that he understood it that any answer to this question would subject -- could subject him to criminal liability, and I'd ask just one more time that you clarify that he understood completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how Mr. Cunningham got that impression, with you I'm perfectly happy if Your Honour wants to repeat the warning. And of course I make it absolutely clear that the suggestion that I was making to him was that he destroyed his notebooks deliberately, knowing that he had taken part in committing criminal actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In addition to what you've said, Ms. Korner, Mr. Cunningham, I said: I think this is the kind of question which, if it causes you this concern that I referred to you before you can ask us to be exempted from answering it. If you feel you can answer that question without exposing yourself to any criminal proceedings or incrimination, then you may proceed. So I mean, I couldn't be more clear than that. I gave him the two options. If you could answer the question without incriminating yourself, go ahead. You don't need to invoke the privilege that is reserved under the Rules. If you think that by answering the question you have concerns about possibly incriminating yourself, then you can ask us for an exemption which I did. But again, I have absolutely no problems with repeating, trying to explain it to him in perhaps clearer terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman's suggestion I think is a very valid one. Perhaps the Court can inquire of the witness as to what was his interpretation of what the Court said to make sure that he understood the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, no problem with that, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break. Actually, we'll reconvene at 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin is here. Everyone is here. Mr. Jokic, I just want to clear this up in my mind. Before we had this break, I was explaining to you following Ms. Korner's question your right to ask to be exempted from answering a question, her question. And you chose to ask to be exempted from answering the question. When I explained to you your right, your privilege, to ask to be exempted and our privilege to say yes or no to you, what did you understand actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that a question which is not -- which is disturbing to me or there are questions to which I do not have to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But disturbing to you why or questions which you do not have to answer, what kind of questions? Let's take them one by one. A question which is disturbing to you, what did you mean? When I explained to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was thinking of the following questions, questions which were disturbing to me or the answer to which I did not know, so I was thinking of future questions that I would not have to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why -- let me go direct straightaway. Why did you ask me to exempt you from answering that question, that particular question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to tell me again what the question was, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was -- the question that Ms. Korner put to you was the following: "Do you think you've taken part in activities, either in the course of your military duties or these attendances of the crisis staff meetings, which might be construed as criminal offences?" This was the question that was put to you. And this is the question that you asked me to exempt you from answering. Why did you ask me to exempt you from answering that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I don't believe that this could have been any criminal act. Nobody ever warned me that this could constitute a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, I see you. I recognise you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to find the Rule because of course the exemption --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The exempt is not absolute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not that. I'm sorry. At the moment, I can't remember what the Rule is, which Rule which Your Honours -- I think it's the standard one in that if the witness feels that -- that's not it either. Your Honour, I ought to know this one by heart. I think it may be Rule 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rule 90(E). A witness may object to making any statement which may tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber, however, may compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in the situation not be used in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Your Honour, I don't know that that was made entirely clear, that the witness's right not to answer the question depends on his belief that it might incriminate himself. And I don't think that's been made perhaps not entirely clear. So I think the witness has now heard this discussion between Your Honours and myself. So I think maybe the question is does the witness believe that to answer that question might incriminate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I had explained to him and which I read before to you. My last words to him before he asked not to answer that question were the following: I think this is the kind of question which if it causes you this concern that I referred you to before you can ask us to be exempted from answering. If you feel you can answer that question without exposing yourself to any criminal proceedings or incrimination, then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, but thank you for your intervention, Ms. Korner. I want to clear this up. Did you ask us to exempt you from answering that question because you believe that answering that question could tend to incriminate you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I address the Court about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think in that case -- if we're going to have further discussion, perhaps the witness should leave Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would agree to that. I would agree to that completely. Let's finish this, and let's have a short discussion between us on how to proceed. Please, I want to put your mind at rest that this is a privilege that you have and which we are recognising. So you don't have to worry about that matter. Usher, could you escort him out for a few minutes, and we will reconvene immediately afterwards. As I understand it, I mean, he's made it quite clear now with the caveat he gave us earlier on, a minute ago, that he was never made aware that certain things done could actually be criminal -- amount to criminal offences. So I think that is the position. But, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I want to express to the Chamber a concern that I have at this point. If the Chamber is of a mind to draw any kind of a conclusion regarding his request to be exempted from answering that question, then I think we've not gone far enough. And I say that for this reason: We need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. I think it's wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have had a very short discussion amongst us on how best to deal with you, and mostly, mostly, our main concern is to protect you as -- to ensure, us three Judges, that your witness rights are fully protected. So I have explained to you what the situation is, and I explained to you also what your rights are. You are going to be asked some further questions by Ms. Korner, and I again repeat to you what I told you before. If by answering any of these questions you sincerely, honestly believe that you might be incriminating yourself or you could tend to incriminate yourself, then just call upon us, and we will consider your request. What we will be doing is we will be distinguishing a little bit between your activities in the military field and your activities inside the ARK Crisis Staff because before, Ms. Korner had pooled them together, and we are now going to separate them. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir, in 1991 when you were in Croatia, you told us you took part in combat operations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There's nothing on the screen in front of me. I just have that remark. I never said I was in Croatia. I was in Mostar, and we carried out our assignments from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's tend to his complaint about the monitor. Usher, could you please... Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I take it also that you also understand a little bit of English. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder how you used to teach the Libyans, the Indonesians and the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbo-Croatian. They spoke our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. You carried out combat operations in Croatia -- in the Croatian conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in respect of that that you feel that answering questions may incriminate you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 you also carried out combat operations in Bosnia, in the war in Bosnia. Do you feel that answering questions about that may incriminate you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: To a large degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also attended in your military capacity the meetings of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina which, as you know, issued decisions. Do you feel that answering questions about that may incriminate you in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you actually destroy your notebooks? I don't think you gave us a date.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I say again I don't know the exact date, but it was after the signing of the Dayton Accords. That is when peace was established there in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and people, including myself, wanted to forget the war as soon as possible. And I felt that a lot of my personal documentation was something that was not -- that I would not need. I didn't want to be burdened with it. I didn't have any private or professional duty to preserve the documents. At the time, I did not destroy them because I was afraid that somebody would do something to me. Simply, it wasn't necessary. I didn't need it any more. And I believe that in future in my life, I wouldn't need it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you destroy your notebooks after the first indictments had been issued by this Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether this was before or after. But at no point did I believe that I had anything to do with the indictments or had any responsibility in relation to the war until in mid-2001 I was invited to talk with the investigators. I didn't believe that I had done anything wrong. And that was not the reason why I destroyed the documents. Perhaps the word "documents" is not -- "destroy" is not quite correct. I simply tore them up and threw them away. So I didn't do that because I felt that I had done anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So your destruction of the notebooks has got nothing to do, you say, with your appreciation that answering questions about your military activities in 1991 and 1992 could incriminate you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you told us that you had no professional responsibility to preserve -- duty to preserve the documents. That's not right, is it, Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It is true that I didn't have any responsibility to do that because had I been obliged to do that, those documents would have been requested of me, and they would have been placed in the archive. So nobody requested those notebooks from me. I didn't destroy any of the unit documents. Perhaps you misunderstood me. These were just my private, working documents, while the documents of the unit are still located in some archive. I don't know where this archive is at the moment, but they're still in the archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood you perfectly, sir. By the fact is you keep saying these are private documents. They weren't. They were military, regulatory documents, weren't they? Documents you were obliged to keep. We have been through that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when the war ended no one requested that I return those documents. And again, the word "documents" is not the right one. It was just my notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was your authorised military workbook, sir, wasn't it? Not a diary and not a personal notebook. That's not go over this all again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he tries to answer this question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we have covered this and we know exactly where we stand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, but there's one further thing, sir. The fact is nobody had to request it, did they? It was your obligation to, when those documents were completed, send it to the military archives to be kept?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No, it was not my obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us, sir, that no one ever explained to you at the beginning of your military service in 1977 or when you became an officer that those notebooks were official documents which it was your obligation to keep and thereafter, when finished, to send to the archives? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to those workbooks or to other documents? Or are you referring only to the workbook?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring now specifically to your officer's workbook.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: In our system, there were two kinds of notebooks. The workbook that we have been discussing now, I didn't have any obligation to return it, this little red notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about your official - whatever the colour - official officer's notebook. Not any private diaries you may have kept yourself, but your official officer's workbook.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I did not have an obligation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So is your answer to my question no one ever informed you that that book, once it was completed, had to be sent for archiving? You're saying that, are you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you told us also a minute ago, you were being -- matters were being explained to you by His Honour, that at the time no one told you that what you were doing was a criminal offence. All I want to ask you is this: Are you now saying that although no one told you, you now appreciate that some of the things you did could be construed as criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not asking him -- I think that's being clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's clear. And I just want to remind him of what I told him before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I believe that certain things can be considered as criminal offences, I don't know. I couldn't tell you. It's only my assumption that they could. But again, I'm just assuming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So really, would your position be this: That as far as you were concerned, you followed without question orders and instructions that were given to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever question an order received through your chain of command from a superior officer to carry out activities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I carried out orders that were issued to me by superior officers. If I properly understand your question, if an order was issued to me by a superior officer, of course I had to carry it out. If you're referring to orders addressed to the unit, we were an organised army like the JNA. And I was under the obligation to carry out orders, to perform a task, an air force task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever question an order, for example, because in your view it was in breach of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that because the discipline maintained in the air force was such that if you'd questioned an order, you would have been removed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, the discipline was such that I would not have been removed, but like in any organised army, orders were not discussed. Once you receive an order as an inferior officer, you were under the obligation to carry it out. If you refused to carry out an order, well, like in any other army, there are disciplinary measures that are undertaken against you. Either against an individual or against a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive, as part of your training, training in the laws and regulations governing warfare?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: During my training as part of my education, yes. During the training, yes. So that would have been between 1974 and 1977 when we underwent such training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include a study of the relevant Geneva Conventions which applied to warfare?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It was really a long time ago. I cannot answer your question with certainty. But I would assume that that included that study as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it from what you say that you received no reminders in 1991 and 1992 of the relevant Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Very, very few. Almost none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What does that mean? Do you mean you were sent a document, or you had a talk that said "remember the relevant conventions"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No specific documents were ever sent. We were cautioned from time to time, but such cautions, if you can understand me in view of the organisation of the army, came from the very top, from the general staff. And they were distributed to all units, including land forces, air forces, and others. They concerned mainly the treatment of prisoners of war who had to be treated in accordance with the relevant provisions of the conventions and so on and so forth. But our case was specific because we, as members of the air force, could not have prisoners of war. So such issues were not given any special attention in our department. It concerned mainly land forces. I couldn't take anyone prisoner from the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in the case of the air force, what was relevant, wasn't it, were the regulations that related to attacks upon civilian population? Those were relevant to the air force, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of reminder, either orally or in writing, about your obligations in respect of attacks upon civilian populations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive any reminders concerning our obligations with respect to attacks because I had never received an order to that effect, that we should engage civilian targets. No. I've never received an order of that kind in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that. But now I want to ask you just in the remaining few minutes for today a little bit about the reporting procedures. It was an obligation, was it not, for you as an officer to make a report to your senior officer on a regular basis as to your activities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: It was not an obligation -- my obligation to write that as an individual. I had to make report on the overall activity of my unit. But there were regular, daily reports which were very brief, mainly that -- mostly about the situation. But there were other, more detailed reports, monthly reports that were sent to the superior command. I was the commander of a squadron. I had an assistant. And he was in charge of composing such reports. He obtained information on the technical affairs, on the human resources and so on and so forth, and this report would be sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we split that. There were short daily reports to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the superior command, and then longer monthly reports. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this right: That both the daily and the monthly reports would be divided into headings or topics?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I think they were divided into several topics, several titles. I don't remember exactly how many, but there were several distinct elements of the report, not only two but more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And they would be divided, for example, into logistics. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Morale in the unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any unusual activity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that. Special observations, unusual things, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The security situation in the area in which the unit was based?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I was not in charge of reporting on the security situation in the area where the unit was stationed. I only had the obligation of describing the security situation within my unit. As for the overall security situation in the area where the unit was billeted, this was taken care of by the logistical unit which had also military police in its ranks. I only had obligations with respect to my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Whoever reported it, whether it was the logistical unit or you in particular, those reports would include, would they not, the political situation, if it might have an impact upon your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: This was perhaps stated in the section dealing with the morale of the unit. It is only logical to assume that the political situation could have an impact on that.
