Again, it's only my assumption. But we were a very small unit, just a squadron, and this could have been the case with respect to the morale, including the political situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to the size of your unit tomorrow. These reporting requirements were strictly enforced weren't they? In other words, those reports had to be sent to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my unit had to send the reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think, as you've already touched upon, discipline in the JNA, and even when it became the VRS in Bosnia, was very strictly enforced?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: The discipline in the JNA was very strict. That is true. However, my personal opinion was that in the last months of the existence of the JNA, the discipline was no longer that strict. And later, and also in the VRS, it was not at a very high level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we put it this way: That you wouldn't take part in an important activity without seeking the approval of your senior officers if it affected clearly the professional nature of your duties? It's not a very good sentence, but you know what I mean, I hope.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to important activities outside the military?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. If you were going to undertake as part of your military duties an activity which was clearly an important one, you did not have, did you, the authority to just agree or not agree without seeking approval?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: As a squadron commander, I never undertook any military activity on my own. I always received orders from my superior command with respect to the use of my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or what you yourself did presumably.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, during that period of time when discipline was no longer at a very high level, when the JNA was falling apart, elements there had remained in these other former republics, so not everything required a specific order from the superior command. And I'm talking about my personal activities here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But involvement, if you wanted to get involved in civilian political activities, that would require the authority, wouldn't it, of your higher command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: I would inform the superior command. I did inform them about the fact that as a member of the crisis staff I had to attend the meetings. Lieutenant Colonel Kostoric who at the time was my superior officer agreed. He had no problem with it. He simply said: "Well, fine. When you have time, you can go and attend those meetings. But if you don't have time for that, try not to burden your unit additionally. If you have any obligations in your unit, then they will come first."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, it's not just that having received the invitation to join this crisis staff you went off and did it; you first of all informed and sought the approval of your senior officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I went for the first time when the officer came to see me. I told him I went to a meeting. I am a member. So before my first attendance, I didn't ask for strict permission. I just went because I didn't believe that I had to ask anyone. And then later when I saw this man, then I simply told him that I'm a member of the crisis staff. And he said: "Very well. I don't have anything against that. But don't let the duties in the unit suffer because of that." Meaning that I would not be present with the unit if the unit had some duties. So the unit had to be number one, and then if I had some space in my duties, had some room or had some free time, then I would be able to go and attend the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we'll take this up, then, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Jokic, we are stopping here for today. I think tomorrow is in the afternoon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're doing this again, are we? Can I be told then, please. I understood us to be in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me check because I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the constant changes in this timetable are just incredible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, I know. Tuesday. No, no, we are in the morning tomorrow. We are in the morning. I apologise, Ms. Korner. We are in the morning in Courtroom III. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no Your Honour. I needn't apologise Your Honour in the slightest. But it wouldn't surprise me to suddenly find we had been changed again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's it. We will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00. You can escort the witness out, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
